title: U.S. consumers remain willing to spend while shifting toward value, selectivity, and financial-risk management as job-security anxiety rises
source_unit: International Council of Shopping Centers, Consumer Economy Report, September 2026
geography: United States households, consumers, workers, retailers, brands, and the consumer economy

observations.period: Spring-summer 2026; spending, inflation attribution, and financial outlook

denominator.unit: U.S. consumers in the summer 2026 ICSC survey

inflation_attribution.unit: percent of consumers whose spending increased citing higher prices, down from 65 percent in spring

financial_outlook.unit: percent expecting their financial situation to improve over the next year

consumer_route.value: continued spending can coexist with lower inflation salience and more deliberate household tradeoffs

observations.method: ICSC quarterly consumer-economy report combining proprietary online surveys and economic data; summer survey fielded July 29-31, 2026.
observations.uncertainty: This is a commercial-industry survey and public summary, not a causal estimate of inflation or income effects; reported shares do not establish actual spending totals or represent all households equally.
observations.subgroup: U.S. consumers, households with different financial cushions, retailers, brands, marketplaces, and services providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher reported spending may reflect prices, essential-cost increases, household composition, or timing rather than stronger real consumption or welfare.

observations.period: Spring-summer 2026; job security and household bargaining

denominator.unit: U.S. consumers in the summer 2026 ICSC survey

job_security.unit: percent feeling secure in their current job, down from 87 percent in spring

job_search.unit: percent of employed consumers planning to look for another job, up from 30 percent in spring

instability_reason.unit: percent citing layoffs or job instability as a reason for seeking new employment, up from 10 percent

work-consumption_route.value: income stability and job security may be becoming more important to consumer choice than inflation alone

observations.method: ICSC comparison of spring and summer 2026 consumer survey responses.
observations.uncertainty: The comparison is descriptive and does not identify whether job anxiety causes shopping changes or how responses differ by occupation, income, or region.
observations.subgroup: Employed consumers, job seekers, households exposed to layoffs, workers with different bargaining power, and employers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Job-search intentions may reflect opportunity-seeking, dissatisfaction, or normal labor-market churn rather than worsening realized employment.

observations.period: Summer-fall 2026; brand loyalty, value, and selective consumption

denominator.unit: U.S. consumers in the summer 2026 ICSC survey

brand_meaning.unit: percent saying brand names mean less today than in the past

trade_down.unit: percent shifting to lower-priced brands or retailers in the prior three months

future_selectivity.unit: percent expecting to become more selective in purchases over the next three months

loyalty_route.value: value-seeking weakens automatic brand loyalty while leaving room for purchases that deliver clear utility, enjoyment, or personal reward

observations.method: ICSC consumer survey questions on brands, retailer switching, deal-seeking, and forward purchase selectivity.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not isolate price, quality, identity, trust, or channel effects, and intentions may not become realized purchase behavior.
observations.subgroup: Price-sensitive households, private-label and branded-product shoppers, retailers, consumer brands, and discretionary-category buyers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Brand loyalty may be changing rather than disappearing; trusted brands can retain value when they make quality and utility legible.

observations.period: Summer-fall 2026; discretionary spending and financial margin

denominator.unit: U.S. consumers in the summer 2026 ICSC survey

nonessential_purchase_intent.unit: percent expecting to make nonessential purchases in the next three months

treat_yourself.unit: percent planning to increase treat-yourself purchases, up from 24 percent in spring

essential_expense_margin.unit: percent saying an essential-expense increase of 249 dollars per month or less would force discretionary cuts

immediate_cutback.unit: percent saying any additional essential-cost increase would require immediate cutbacks

open_test.value: consumer resilience may be conditional: households preserve small rewards while operating with limited room for additional shocks

observations.method: ICSC survey comparison of discretionary purchase intentions and household responses to essential-cost increases.
observations.uncertainty: These are self-reported expectations, not observed budgets or longitudinal financial outcomes; the report does not establish debt, savings, housing, care, or regional mechanisms for each household.
observations.subgroup: Households with different savings, debt, housing, care, and essential-expense burdens; discretionary retailers and service providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Selective indulgence can reflect adaptation and agency, but it may also mask reduced security or borrowing when essential costs rise.

related_sources.claim: Ipsos consumer-confidence work provides cross-national macro-consumer context complementary to the U.S. household tradeoff evidence.
Mondelēz State of Snacking provides complementary social, cultural, and discretionary-consumption context.

boundary: This record adds a U.S. consumer-economy route from job security and household financial margin through value-seeking, brand switching, discretionary spending, and selective resilience. It uses a commercial survey and economic context, not respondent-level records in the corpus, causal household-budget analysis, observed transactions, or proof of welfare improvement.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ICSC September 10, 2026 report announcement was reviewed for survey field dates, sample sizes, spending, inflation attribution, job security, brand switching, discretionary spending, and financial-margin findings.
